## Claude synthesis

### Overall Assessment: Useful with Caveats

Cleveland and Lukes overlay the digitized 1935–40 HOLC "redlining" maps on 2018–19 school-district boundaries and school locations in 144 metropolitan areas and run enrollment-weighted, CBSA-fixed-effects difference-in-means regressions of district revenue, school expenditure, school racial composition, and SEDA achievement on HOLC grade, with D as the reference. The cross-sectional core is credible and worth citing: within the same metro, schools sitting inside formerly D-graded polygons enroll far more Black (36% vs. 22% in A polygons) and far fewer White students (14% vs. 44%), and score 0.64 SD lower than schools in A polygons (Table 5), with a monotone A–B–C–D gradient that holds in every region; districts composed mostly of D-graded land raise roughly half the local revenue per pupil of A districts (\$5,240 vs. an A–D gap of \$5,937), with state and federal aid closing about three-quarters of that gap (Table 2). Those level gaps are large, precisely estimated, and unlikely to be overturned by the design's known weaknesses. The rest of the paper needs qualification. First, the design is a raw within-metro contrast with no controls; since HOLC grades encoded the race, class, and housing stock neighborhoods already had in the 1930s (the paper says so on p.20), the A–D gaps bundle pre-existing differences with anything the maps added, and the paper never asks whether grade predicts outcomes conditional on current neighborhood SES. The Methods section calls the approach "conservative" and "correlational" (pp.9–10) and the Discussion says "not causal" (p.21), but the abstract ("the consequences of redlining persist today"), the introduction, and the policy section ("redlining's impacts on property values") say otherwise; readers should follow the Methods, not the abstract. Second, the published article contains an exhibit error unusual for a peer-reviewed journal: Figure 3, captioned as district per-pupil revenue in 2018 dollars from 1989 to 2018, is not a revenue figure. Its y-axes run 0.20–0.85, three of its four panels are pixel-for-pixel the Percent Black, Percent White, and Simpson's Index panels of Figure 4, its "federal revenue" panel shows A districts highest (the reverse of Table 2), and its four decadal points cannot contain the "2009–2010 spike" the text describes. Every finance-trend claim in the paper, including the Discussion's "persistent and growing over time from the 1980s to 2018," therefore rests on a supplemental table that does not travel with the PDF. Third, the prose misreports the tables in several places a reader is likely to quote: a Northeast D-school score of "−0.023 SD" that is −0.225 in Table 5; Midwest school spending gaps called "statistically significant" that carry no stars; "virtually no statistically significant differences" in test-score trends when all three national coefficients are significant at p<.01; state/local school spending gaps called "insignificant" in the Discussion that the Results and Table 3 show as significant; and a Table 1 performance sample of 5,124 schools against Table 5 Ns of 6,890, 5,193, and 6,183. Fourth, the paper's most interesting substantive result, that schools in D polygons spend the most per pupil even though D districts raise the least (Table 3 vs. Table 2), is under-sold, never reconciled with a school-level district-fixed-effects model, and omitted from the abstract, whose title word "Funding" invites the opposite reading. There is no data or code statement despite fully public inputs. The right posture is: cite the paper for the within-metro descriptive gaps in Tables 2, 4, and 5, quoting numbers from the tables rather than the text; do not cite it for finance trends over time, for causal effects of the HOLC maps, for property values as the mechanism, or for "underfunded" schools in redlined neighborhoods; and treat the 2021 EdWorkingPaper version (ai21-363) as the first public statement of these findings.

#### Key Strengths

- A new, reusable linkage at scale: HOLC polygons joined to 1,760 districts and roughly 9,000–9,700 schools across 144 CBSAs, entirely from public data (Mapping Inequality, TIGER/Line, NCES EDGE and CCD, F-33, NERD\$, SEDA 4.0), with an explicit area-weighting formula and discretization cutpoints (p.10). Others can extend it.
- The cross-sectional level gaps are large, precisely estimated, monotone across grades, and consistent across all four Census regions: an A–D average-score gap of 0.643 SD (SE 0.04; regional range 0.541–0.753) (Table 5), A–D gaps of −0.14 in share Black and +0.30 in share White (Table 4), and an A–D local-revenue gap of \$5,937 (SE \$1,228), significant in every region (Table 2).
- Tables 2–5 are complete and internally consistent: coefficients, CBSA-clustered SEs, R², F, and N for every model; regional Ns sum exactly to national Ns in every panel; and the federal, state, and local revenue coefficients in Table 2 sum to the total-revenue coefficients.
- The district-revenue versus school-expenditure contrast (Table 2 vs. Table 3) is genuinely informative for school-finance readers: D districts raise about half the local revenue of A districts, intergovernmental aid closes roughly three-quarters of the gap, and schools located in D polygons then spend somewhat more per pupil than schools in A polygons (\$16,890 vs. an A gap of −\$1,539).
- The literature review is broad and current across HOLC economics, public health, school finance, and desegregation, and the paper includes a section on reasons the relationship might not exist (desegregation, Great Migration, school finance reforms; pp.6–7).

#### Key Concerns

- Figure 3 (p.13) is the wrong figure. Its panels A, B, and D reproduce Figure 4's Percent Black, Percent White, and Simpson's Index series under revenue titles; panel C (0.40–0.83) is consistent with share non-White and matches nothing else in the article; the axes cannot be 2018 dollars given Table 2's \$14,402 total-revenue constant. The longitudinal finance narrative (pp.13–14) and the Discussion's "persistent and growing" claim (p.20) have no displayed support; the coefficients exist only in Supplemental Table A4(A).
- The causal framing outruns the design. The model is a within-CBSA difference in means with no covariates (p.10); HOLC grades recorded neighborhood race, class, and building stock as of the 1930s (p.20); and the revisionist HOLC literature the paper cites (Fishback et al., 2020; Aaronson, Hartley, and Mazumder, 2021; Hillier, 2003; Michney, 2022) finds that the maps explain only a modest share of later differences. Property values, the asserted mechanism for the revenue gap, are never measured. The abstract, introduction, and policy section nonetheless speak of "consequences," "impacts," and policies that "continue to shape" outcomes.
- The prose cannot be trusted for specific numbers. Confirmed text-versus-table errors: Northeast D-school score −0.023 vs. −0.225 (p.18 vs. Table 5); Midwest school PPE gaps of \$302 and \$202 called significant but unstarred (p.14 vs. Table 3); "virtually no statistically significant differences" in test-score trends vs. A/B/C all p<.01 (p.18 vs. Table 5); state/local PPE gaps called "insignificant" (p.20) vs. B −\$1,010* and C −\$745** (Table 3); "smallest between A and C (\$141)" for a D–C contrast of −\$141 (p.14); D districts said to receive more federal revenue than A–C districts (pp.3, 20) when C districts receive \$253 more (p<.01); "across all four Regions" total revenue lower for D districts when West B districts have \$1,082 less (p<.01); "in every Region" D schools more Black and less diverse when West share-Black and Northeast Simpson contrasts are all insignificant (p.21 vs. Table 4). The Table 1 performance sample (5,124 schools) does not match any N in Table 5 (6,890/5,193/6,183), and the Figure 2 legend says 141 CBSAs while its note says 144.
- The Figure 4 time-series text does not match the printed figure. The D–A share-Black gap is described as shrinking from 13.4 to 10.3 points; the plot shows roughly 10 points at both ends. The A–D share-White gap is described as "around 35 percentage points"; the plot shows roughly 27–29. The Simpson's gaps are said to have "surpassed −0.08"; the plot shows roughly 0.05–0.06. The same page says D-school diversity gaps "continued to grow" and, a paragraph later, that D schools are "converging." Whether the quoted numbers come from a fixed-effects specification in Supplemental Table A4(B) is not stated.
- The finance story is internally unresolved and the total-funding claim is fragile. The national A–D and B–D total-revenue gaps are significant only at p<.10 (\$1,546, SE \$822; \$992, SE \$536) and not significant in any region (Table 2); schools in D polygons spend more, not less (Table 3); the Title I explanation cannot account for D schools also having higher state/local spending; and the within-district allocation argument rests on supplemental figures (A6, A7, A10) that do not travel with the article. No school-level model with district fixed effects is reported.
- Inference and measurement are weaker in the regional results. The West has 15 CBSA clusters and the Northeast 30, enrollment weights concentrate influence in a few large districts, no few-cluster correction is reported, and some SEs are implausibly small (Northeast share-Black B coefficient −0.11, SE 0.006). A district enters the sample on any polygon overlap and is graded on the HOLC-covered part of its land area only, so "D district" means "mostly D among its graded area," and the size of the D reference group by region is only in an unavailable supplement.
- Reproducibility is below journal-era norms for a fully-public-data paper: no data or code availability statement, no replication package, no software named, and sample-defining steps that the authors' 2021 working paper documented (NYC sub-districts, point-assigned charter LEAs, dropped E-graded polygons, OLS vs. EB SEDA estimates, race-category count for Simpson's index) are absent from the published article. Mapping Inequality has since moved to a 2023 release with more than 100 additional maps, so a replicator downloading today starts from a different HOLC universe.

#### What to Rely On

- Within the same metro, schools located inside 1930s D-graded polygons today enroll student bodies that are about 36% Black and 14% White nationally (Table 4 constants), and schools in A polygons are 14 points less Black and 30 points more White (Table 4, A rows: −0.14, SE 0.027; 0.30, SE 0.022). The gradient is monotone across grades. Regional exception: in the West, D-polygon schools are 9% Black and the A/B/C share-Black contrasts are all insignificant.
- Schools in D polygons post average math/ELA scores 0.643 SD (SE 0.04) below schools in A polygons nationally, with regional A–D gaps of 0.541–0.753 SD and a monotone gradient (Table 5, first panel). Quote the SD units; the "just over 1.9 grade levels" conversion (p.18) has no stated factor.
- Districts composed mostly of D-graded land raise far less local revenue per pupil: D constant \$5,240 against A–D, B–D, and C–D gaps of \$5,937, \$4,592, and \$1,713, all p<.01 nationally, with the A–D local gap significant in every region (Table 2). State aid offsets much of it (A–D −\$3,670, SE \$752; B–D −\$3,210), and federal aid offsets some (A–D −\$722; B–D −\$391), leaving a net national total-revenue gap of about \$1,546 (p<.10).
- Schools in D polygons have higher nominal per-pupil expenditures than schools in A, B, or C polygons: constant \$16,890 with gaps of −\$1,539 (p<.10), −\$1,313 (p<.05), and −\$882 (p<.01) (Table 3), including higher federal expenditures (−\$602 vs. A, p<.01). The local-revenue shortfall sits at the district level, not in nominal school-level spending.
- Learning rates (within-cohort grade slopes) differ little by HOLC grade nationally (A 0.006, SE 0.006; B 0.008 and C 0.005 at p<.10; Table 5, second panel), so the achievement gap is a gap in levels, consistent with student composition rather than school effectiveness.
- The linkage method itself: area-weighted district grades with cutpoints at 1.5/2.5/3.5 and point-in-polygon school grades (p.10), and the finding that a schools'-average district grade correlates 0.91–0.93 with the area-weighted measure (p.13).

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- "The consequences of redlining persist today" and any reading of the gaps as effects of the HOLC maps — the design is a no-controls within-metro contrast; the grades recorded pre-existing 1930s conditions; the causal HOLC literature (Aaronson, Hartley, and Mazumder, 2021; Fishback et al., 2020) uses boundary and comparison-city designs precisely because raw grade contrasts are confounded, and finds partial, fading map effects. Cite this paper for description, those papers for causation.
- District finance gaps "persistent and growing over time from the 1980s to 2018" (p.20) and everything in the longitudinal finance paragraphs (pp.13–14), including the 2009–10 ARRA spike — the printed Figure 3 is a relabeled copy of the racial-diversity figure and the underlying coefficients (Supplemental Table A4(A)) are not in the article. Unverifiable as published.
- The Figure 4 trend numbers (13.4 to 10.3 points, "around 35 percentage points," gaps "surpassed −0.08") — none can be read off the printed figure, and the page contradicts itself on whether D-school diversity gaps grew or converged. Check Supplemental Table A4(B) before quoting any of them.
- "Districts composed of A to C neighborhoods are better funded" (p.3) — the national total-revenue gaps are p<.10, no regional A–D total gap is significant, West B districts have significantly less than D districts, and schools in D polygons spend more. The robust statement is the local-revenue gap.
- "Districts with D neighborhoods receive more federal Title I funding" (p.3) and federal/state funds "favor D districts relative to A to C districts" (pp.12, 20) — only total federal revenue is observed, and C districts receive \$253 more of it than D districts (p<.01; Table 2). The D–C state difference is insignificant.
- Schools in these areas "predominantly educate Black ... students" (abstract) — 36% nationally, 47–48% in the Midwest and South, 9% in the West (Table 4). "Predominantly non-White and low-income" is supported; "predominantly Black" is not.
- "Virtually no statistically significant differences" in test-score trends (p.18) and the Discussion's "do not reveal whether the gaps have changed over time" (p.21) — the national cohort-trend contrasts are all significant at p<.01 (A 0.010, B 0.007, C 0.004; Table 5) and imply the A–D gap widened across 2009–2018 cohorts, though the magnitudes are small.
- Any specific number quoted from the prose rather than the tables — confirmed slips include −0.023 vs. −0.225 (Northeast), the Midwest \$302/\$202 "significant" claim, the "between A and C (\$141)" label, the p.20 "insignificant" state/local claim, the "across all four Regions" and "in every Region" generalizations, Table 1's 5,124 vs. Table 5's 6,890, and Figure 2's 141 vs. 144.
- Regional estimates, especially the West (15 CBSAs, 159 districts) and South (45 CBSAs, 187 districts) — few clusters, enrollment weighting, no small-sample correction, and many p<.10 stars; re-read the table before citing any regional coefficient.
- The property-value mechanism and the policy implications (decoupling revenue from property taxes, METCO-style transfers, HOLC-based targeting; pp.22–23) — no property-value, assessed-value, or tax-base data are used, no mechanism is tested, and the recommendation of "additional resources" for D-neighborhood schools does not engage Table 3's finding that those schools already spend the most.
- "This article is the first to document the relationship between HOLC grades and modern educational outcomes" (p.22) — the same findings circulated as EdWorkingPaper 21-363 in November 2021 (uncited); Baker, Di Carlo, and Green (2022), cited four times for other purposes, mapped HOLC grades onto district composition and funding adequacy in seven metros; Aaronson et al. (2023), cited on p.5, studied children's educational attainment. Fair as "first national, multi-outcome K–12 analysis."
- Several background citations do not support the claims attached to them — Baker-Smith (2018), a study of suspension policy, for property values in majority-minority neighborhoods (p.20); Hoffman et al. (2020), on urban heat, for property values and demographics (p.2); Baum-Snow and Lutz (2011), on residential location, for causal effects of segregation on school funding and achievement (p.3). The p.2 claim that "most district revenue comes from local sources" is contradicted by p.5 (state 45–47%; property taxes 36%).
- Every robustness check and the FRPL result (79.3% in D schools; A–D −0.37) — all live only in the unavailable supplement (Tables A5–A8, Figures A5–A7, A10); the covariate check in Supplemental Table A7, arguably the most legacy-relevant test in the project, gets one sentence.

## Codex synthesis

### Overall Assessment: Useful With Caveats

This paper provides useful descriptive evidence that historical HOLC grades remain associated with district revenues, school racial composition, and average achievement in the mapped institutions studied. Its most informative qualification is that lower local revenues in D-classified districts coexist with higher expenditures at schools located in D neighborhoods; these are different units and comparisons (p. 12, Table 2; p. 15, Table 3). The achievement and composition gradients are also supported by the published tables (p. 16, Table 4; p. 19, Table 5). My judgment is that these findings warrant selective citation as weighted, within-CBSA associations, but do not establish the causal effects of redlining, the proposed mechanisms, or the effectiveness of remedies. The adequate methods, literature, and contribution assessments are compatible with weak writing and reproducibility assessments: interpretable cross-sectional tables survive consequential reporting errors, an unusable longitudinal finance figure, and incomplete documentation. Read the tables with their notes rather than relying on the abstract or discussion alone; verify the intended finance exhibit and supporting materials before building on funding-trend claims.

#### Key Strengths

- The linkage brings district finance, school spending, racial composition, and achievement into a common historical geographic framework using identified administrative and research datasets. This is a useful empirical integration across school-finance, segregation, and neighborhood literatures (pp. 3–10).
- The main tables disclose the D reference category, CBSA fixed effects, outcome-specific weights, clustered standard errors, and regional estimates, making the central descriptive comparisons inspectable (p. 12, Table 2; p. 15, Table 3; p. 16, Table 4; p. 19, Table 5).
- Separating district revenues from school expenditures reveals an important difference that a uniform account of funding disadvantage would miss; lower district revenue does not imply lower spending at every school in a D polygon (p. 12, Table 2; p. 15, Table 3).
- The paper distinguishes average achievement from learning and cohort trends, discusses forces that could weaken historical associations, and explicitly acknowledges its correlational design (pp. 6–9, 21). These qualifications support careful use even where the broader framing overreaches.

#### Key Concerns

- Historical attribution exceeds the design. The abstract says, ‘the consequences of redlining persist today’ (p. 1), while the discussion states, ‘this article’s results are not causal’ (p. 21). Grades incorporate prior neighborhood disadvantage; metropolitan fixed effects do not isolate their causal influence. District classifications summarize mapped land, and school classifications use building locations rather than student residences (p. 10). My judgment is that both causal interpretation and generalization beyond the included institutions require substantial qualification.
- The finance-trend figure is defective. Figure 3’s ‘A. Per-Pupil Total Revenue,’ ‘B. Per-Pupil Federal Revenue,’ and ‘D. Per-Pupil Local Revenue’ reproduce trajectories labeled ‘A. Percent Black,’ ‘B. Percent White,’ and ‘C. Simpson’s Diversity Index’ in Figure 4 (p. 13, Figure 3; p. 17, Figure 4). This verified exhibit mismatch prevents checking the finance narrative; it does not establish that the underlying regressions are wrong. The supporting coefficients are assigned to an unavailable online appendix (p. 23, note 3).
- Several prose summaries misstate the tabulated evidence. The text calls Midwest school-spending contrasts ‘statistically significant higher spending’ (p. 14), but Table 3 prints A ‘\$302 (\$555)’ and B ‘\$202 (\$630)’ without stars (p. 15). It also claims ‘virtually no statistically significant differences’ for national learning rates and score trends (p. 18), whereas the score-change rows are A ‘0.01*** (0.003),’ B ‘0.007*** (0.002),’ and C ‘0.004*** (0.001),’ with ‘***p < .01’ (p. 19, Table 5). Small magnitudes must not be described as statistical insignificance.
- Reproducibility is limited by unresolved samples and construction choices. Table 1 reports performance ‘Schools 5124’ (p. 9), but Table 5 reports ‘N 6890,’ ‘N 5193,’ and ‘N 6183’ across its performance outcomes (p. 19), without reconciling the overview count. No replication package or execution environment is identified in the supplied article, and spatial crosswalk and longitudinal harmonization details are incomplete (pp. 7–10, 13, 17, 23). Online supplements are not bound into the PDF and are unavailable here; reported robustness is not independently verified.
- The literature provides useful context, but priority and attribution need checking. The defensible contribution is the combined institutional analysis; the claim to be ‘the first to document the relationship between HOLC grades and modern educational outcomes’ (p. 22) needs narrower scope given the paper’s own account of earlier attainment research (pp. 4–5). A concrete citation mismatch is visible: ‘majority-minority neighborhoods are more likely to have lower property values’ cites Baker-Smith (p. 20), whose listed article is ‘Suspensions suspended: Do changes to high school suspension policies change suspension rates?’ (p. 24). This flags a citation problem, not a refutation of the property-value claim.

#### What to Rely On

- Higher local district revenue in higher HOLC categories within the sample: the national A–D contrast is \$5,937 per pupil (SE \$1,228; p < .01), while the total-revenue contrast is \$1,546 (SE \$822; only p < .10), in inflation-adjusted dollars (p. 12, Table 2). The local-revenue evidence is more precise than the total-revenue contrast.
- School spending can run in the opposite direction from district revenue: the national A–D total-expenditure contrast is −\$1,539 per pupil (SE \$852; only p < .10), and B–D and C–D contrasts are also negative, with stronger statistical support (p. 15, Table 3). This supports distinguishing units, not an identified within-district allocation mechanism.
- The national school-composition comparisons show smaller Black enrollment shares, larger White enrollment shares, and greater within-school racial diversity in A, B, and C locations relative to D (p. 16, Table 4). Regional exceptions matter, and Simpson’s index does not by itself measure segregation between schools.
- Schools located in A polygons have substantially higher average achievement than those in D polygons: the national contrast is 0.643 SD (SE 0.040; p < .01), with positive contrasts across the regional estimates (p. 19, Table 5). This is aggregate test performance, not school effectiveness or individual learning loss caused by redlining.

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- Causal effects, mediation, and policy prescriptions: the comparisons do not separate historical grading from prior disadvantage or later sorting, estimate spending adequacy, show that reforms failed, or establish which intervention would close gaps (pp. 9–10, 20–23).
- Persistent or widening district funding gaps: the printed finance figure cannot substantiate these trajectories, and the intended exhibit and supplementary coefficient table need verification (p. 13, Figure 3; pp. 13–14; p. 23, note 3).
- Claims of equal learning or absent score trends: the outcomes summarize school-level grade and cohort slopes, and the published national score-change contrasts are statistically detectable; they do not establish individual learning equivalence (p. 8; p. 19, Table 5).
- Population-wide or universal regional conclusions: mapped district land and school locations are exposure proxies, outcome samples differ, and national patterns do not hold uniformly across regional comparisons (pp. 9–10; pp. 12, 15–16, Tables 2–4).
- Exact demographic trend gaps and the writing review’s claim of late ‘narrowing relative to A and B’: Figure 4 shows D-school diversity rising late, but the D–A gap looks approximately unchanged and the D–B gap appears to widen, so the sub-review’s narrowing interpretation is not supported (p. 17, Figure 4, panel C). Exact magnitudes require the unavailable supplemental coefficients; neither rising diversity nor these group trajectories establishes a policy effect.
- Claims of historical priority or a settled mechanism: the article’s literature supports contextualization, but its institutional linkage should not be cited as discovery of the broad housing–education relationship. The literature sub-review’s external-source assessments were not independently rechecked in this synthesis, and no field-wide priority finding is adopted (pp. 3–7, 22).

#### Verification notes

- CONFIRMED — Methods/contribution finance contrasts and precision: national A–D local revenue \$5,937 (SE \$1,228; p < .01), total revenue \$1,546 (SE \$822; p < .10), and school expenditure −\$1,539 (SE \$852; p < .10) match the printed tables (p. 12, Table 2; p. 15, Table 3).
- CONFIRMED — Methods/contribution demographic and achievement patterns match Tables 4–5; the national achievement A–D coefficient is 0.643 SD (SE 0.040; p. 19, Table 5), with regional qualifications for composition (p. 16, Table 4).
- CONFIRMED — The methods, writing, contribution, and reproducibility reviews correctly identify the duplicated finance/demographic trajectories under incompatible labels (p. 13, Figure 3; p. 17, Figure 4), as quoted above.
- CONFIRMED — The methods/writing significance objections match the paper: the Midwest spending prose and national score-trend prose conflict with the quoted cells above (p. 14 versus p. 15, Table 3; p. 18 versus p. 19, Table 5).
- CONFIRMED — Methods/writing/reproducibility sample mismatch: ‘Schools 5124’ in the performance overview versus ‘N 6890,’ ‘N 5193,’ and ‘N 6183’ in the outcome regressions remains unexplained (p. 9, Table 1; p. 19, Table 5).
- CONFIRMED — Reproducibility/writing weighting discrepancy: ‘All outcomes are weighted for district or school enrollment’ (p. 10) differs from ‘total number of math and ELA tests for pooled SEDA estimates’ (p. 19, Table 5 note); use the table-specific description for achievement.
- CORRECTED — Writing review’s ‘narrowing relative to A and B’ is unsupported: D diversity rises late, but visual inspection suggests an approximately stable D–A gap and widening D–B gap (p. 17, Figure 4C); exact coefficients are unavailable, and the sub-review’s narrowing claim is not propagated.
- CONFIRMED — Literature review’s Baker-Smith claim/reference mismatch is present on pp. 20 and 24, with both passages quoted above; this check establishes the mismatch in the article, not the cited study’s complete contents.
- COULD NOT CHECK — Supplementary robustness, longitudinal coefficients, and detailed finance reconciliation: the article directs readers to online materials (pp. 12–15, 19–20, 23) that are not bound into this PDF and are unavailable for this review.

#### Per-Dimension Ratings

| Dimension | Rating | Confidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Methods | adequate | high (0.90) |
| Literature | adequate | high (0.88) |
| Writing | weak | high (0.98) |
| Contribution | adequate | high (0.91) |
| Reproducibility | weak | high (0.94) |
